sections.title: Neurocognitive Disorder Scales
sections.text:
Major Neurocognitive Disorder and Mild Neurocognitive Disorder are both scored from the items of all six neurocognitive domains; the two scales share the same items and differ in their severity thresholds.
The six neurocognitive domains correspond to the cognitive domains on which the DSM-5 neurocognitive disorders are defined. Each domain is measured by between two and seven items, all of which also contribute to the hierarchy and to the DSM-5 disorder scales.
Complex attention
Executive function
Language
Learning and memory
Perceptual-motor
Social cognition

sections.title: MAPsy Scoring
sections.text:
The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.
The score itself is not displayed in the report: it is converted to a percentile and assigned a severity band, and the report presents those.
For the Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features scale, the items measuring Anxiousness and Withdrawal are reverse scored before summing, so that low anxiousness and low withdrawal contribute to the scale in the direction that defines the disorder.

sections.title: MAPsy Percentiles
sections.text:
Percentiles are the primary metric for presenting scores because they are comparable across constructs, regardless of the number of items, and are readily communicated to clients and other professionals. Each score is converted to a percentile against the distribution of scores on that construct in a reference sample drawn from Forbes et al.’s (2025) study. Percentiles can be based on the whole reference sample, All (respondents aged 16 years and over), or on one of two subsets of it, Youth (16 to 24 years) and Adult (25 years and over). The Youth or Adult sample is selected by default from the client’s age at administration, calculated from their date of birth, and the Adult sample is used when no date of birth is entered.
The reference sample is best described as a distress-enriched sample: most of its members were receiving mental health treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community. A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community. A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.
The percentile does not itself say whether a level of psychopathology is clinically significant; that judgement is carried by the severity band. The percentile instead shows how far the client’s level of psychopathology is from what is typical of the reference sample.

sections.title: MAPsy Severity Bands
sections.text:
Each construct’s score is assigned a severity band. The three bands are:
Not Elevated: Symptoms are absent or at a level that does not, on its own, warrant clinical attention; the construct is unlikely to be a focus of formulation or treatment.
Elevated: Symptoms are at a level that a clinician would want to know about and that may inform case formulation, but may not be central to the client’s presentation. An Elevated score identifies an area worth exploring in the interview.
Clinically Significant: Symptoms are at a level that is likely to be important to the client’s presentation and that warrants further assessment.
The bands are separated by two thresholds on the construct’s score, which are specific to each construct. For the spectra, subspectra, subfactors, clusters, personality facets, and neurocognitive domains, the thresholds are the sums of their items’ thresholds, which were set by clinical review of each item’s content. For some constructs, the two thresholds are the same, so there is no Elevated band.
For the DSM-5 disorder scales, the thresholds were based on how common each disorder is in the general population, not on item thresholds. A more prevalent disorder therefore generally reaches a band at a lower percentile than a less prevalent one. For example, against the Adult reference sample, a client at the 73rd percentile on the Major Depressive Disorder scale is in the Clinically Significant band, while a client at the 92nd percentile on the Panic Disorder scale is in the Elevated band. The severity band, not the percentile, is therefore the comparison to use across disorder scales. A band on a DSM-5 disorder scale describes the level of the symptoms that the MAPsy measures for that disorder and does not establish a diagnosis.

sections.title: MAPsy Report
sections.text:
The report presents a client’s results in two frameworks.
The Empirical Hierarchy panel shows the nine spectra, each expanding to its subspectra, subfactors, clusters, and items. Four buttons control what is shown: Collapse All shows the spectra closed; Focused shows elevated constructs, except those beneath a Not Elevated construct; Elevated+ shows every elevated construct, with Not Elevated constructs dimmed or hidden; and Expand All opens every spectrum down to its clusters.
The DSM Disorders panel lists the disorder scales by the severity band of the client’s score: Clinically Significant, then Elevated, then Not Elevated. Each scale expands to the clusters, facets, or domains from which it is scored. The Collapse All button shows the disorder scales closed, and Expand All opens them.
In both panels, each row has a bar showing the severity bands, with a marker at the client’s percentile. Below the two panels, the Interpretation panel names the elevated spectra, subspectra, subfactors, and disorder scales, and, in the four spectra without subfactors, the elevated clusters.
A Risk of Self-harm or Suicide panel appears at the top of the report whenever the client has endorsed any of the four suicidality items, and lists each such item with the response selected.

sections.title: Development of the MAPsy
sections.text: The MAPsy is built on the item pool and empirical structure published by Forbes et al. (2025), who extracted candidate symptoms from the DSM-5 text, developed a survey of 680 items, administered it to 14,762 respondents, and derived a consensus structure of 27 subfactors, two subspectra, and eight spectra. The items retained were those that best measured each cluster and subfactor, judged on their readability, face validity, response distributions, and correlations with the constructs they contribute to. The MAPsy scores nine spectra, one more than the consensus structure, because confirmatory factor analysis of its items showed Mania and Detachment to be empirically distinct.

sections.title: MAPsy Reference Sample
sections.text:
The reference sample for the percentiles, and the sample in which the psychometric properties below were examined, comprises the 6,883 respondents in Forbes et al.’s (2025) study who took the full-length survey and were presented with every item. Forbes et al. surveyed respondents aged 16 years and over between December 2020 and October 2022, recruited through social media advertising, Australian community groups, and an undergraduate student pool at Macquarie University.
By gender, 52.4 percent of the reference sample selected female, 33.7 percent male, 9.5 percent non-binary, gender fluid, or another identity, 2.6 percent more than one of these, and 1.8 percent none of these. By age, 32.5 percent were aged 16 to 24 years (n = 2,238; the Youth reference sample), 24.2 percent 25 to 39 years, 30.3 percent 40 to 59 years, and 13.0 percent 60 years or over; the 4,645 respondents aged 25 years and over form the Adult reference sample. Respondents resided in Australia (48.5 percent), the United States (21.0 percent), and other or unreported countries (30.5 percent).
The sample reported a high level of psychological distress. At the time of the survey, 67.6 percent were receiving medication or psychological therapy for a mental health problem, and on the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10; Kessler et al., 2002) the median score was 31, with 56.3 percent scoring 30 or above, the range indicating very high distress (Andrews & Slade, 2001).
Separate Youth and Adult reference samples were adopted because respondents aged 16 to 24 score higher than those aged 25 and over on most constructs, and the difference between these two groups accounts for most of the variation in scores across the four age groups; gender-specific reference samples were not adopted, because differences between female and male respondents are small across constructs.

sections.title: MAPsy Factor Structure
sections.text:
The MAPsy’s cluster structure reproduces the spectra of Forbes et al.’s published structure, most closely for Externalising, Thought Disorder, and Neurodevelopmental and Cognitive Difficulties and least closely for Harmful Substance Use.
Model fit. Each spectrum was fitted as a confirmatory factor model on its own items, with subfactors specified as correlated factors within the five spectra that have them, using weighted least squares (WLSMV) estimation on polychoric correlations in the 4,835 reference-sample respondents with complete data on every item. All nine models converged. Mania (CFI = .99, RMSEA = .05) and Harmful Substance Use (CFI = .98, RMSEA = .08) fit well, Somatoform (CFI = .92) and Thought Disorder (CFI = .90) fit acceptably, and Externalising (CFI = .85) and Eating Pathology (CFI = .88) fit marginally; Eating Pathology’s RMSEA of .19 reflects the small size of its seven-item model. Internalising (CFI = .78) and Detachment (CFI = .77) fit poorly on CFI. In Internalising, the four subfactors are distinct (correlations from .50 to .76) and the misfit arises from dependence among items across its 51 items; in Detachment, the single factor is defined by its depressed mood and reclusiveness items (loadings from .70 to .90), while the three items specific to detachment (restricted emotional expression, low sexual interest, and romantic avoidance) load between .41 and .50 and correlate with one another beyond the factor. The Neurodevelopmental and Cognitive Difficulties model converged, but its information matrix could not be inverted, so only its SRMR (.04) is available.
Distinctness of the subfactors. Within each spectrum the subfactors are empirically distinct, with two exceptions. In Neurodevelopmental and Cognitive Difficulties, the three items of the Forgetfulness subfactor also load on Neurocognitive Impairment (loadings from .65 to .69), leaving Forgetfulness with little variance of its own. In Somatoform, Somatic Symptoms and Dysregulated Sleep, a subfactor of two items, correlate .97. Forgetfulness and Dysregulated Sleep are retained as subfactors in keeping with the consensus structure.
Mania and Detachment as separate spectra. Mania and Detachment are scored as separate spectra because, when Forbes et al.’s Mania/Low Detachment spectrum was fitted on its 19 items with its three subfactors as correlated factors, the Mania and Detachment factors were uncorrelated (r = −.05).
Congruence with the published structure. The congruence of the MAPsy’s cluster structure with the published structure was examined by principal components analysis of the 95 clusters with oblimin rotation, comparing the component loadings with those reported by Forbes et al. for their primary and hold-out samples using Tucker’s congruence coefficient, for which values of .95 and above indicate good agreement and values from .85 to .95 fair agreement. Externalising (.97 against the primary sample, .94 against the hold-out sample), Thought Disorder (.95, .89), and Neurodevelopmental and Cognitive Difficulties (.95, .89) reproduce the published spectra closely. Internalising (.80, .79), Mania/Low Detachment (.80, .87), Somatoform (.75, primary sample only), and Eating Pathology (.81, hold-out sample only) reproduce them less closely, and Harmful Substance Use (.57, hold-out sample only) least; Somatoform’s coefficient reflects the proportion of its published content that is not carried in the retained items, including all of its content on elimination symptoms, sleep apnoea, and sexual dysfunction. For comparison, the median congruence between Forbes et al.’s own primary and hold-out samples across their 36 constructs is .70, and against that calibration every spectrum except Harmful Substance Use reproduces its published counterpart at least as closely as Forbes et al.’s structure replicated between their own two samples.

sections.title: MAPsy Agreement with the Starting Item Pool
sections.text:
Scores from the 154 retained items agree closely with scores from the full 549-item starting pool at every level of the hierarchy and on the disorder scales, and somewhat less closely on the facets, the domains, and the Mania spectrum.
Comparison with the starting item pool. Every construct was scored twice for the same respondents, from the 154 retained items and from the 549-item starting pool, and the two scores were compared by Spearman’s rank correlation and by the median absolute difference between the two percentiles per respondent (per-construct n from 4,835 to 5,784). The median correlation was .97 for the seven spectra other than Mania and Detachment, .97 for the subspectra, .94 for the subfactors, .89 for the 76 clusters that do not retain every item of their starting-pool counterpart, and .94 for the 24 disorder scales scored from clusters. For a typical construct, half of respondents differ by no more than 6.5 percentile points between the two scorings.
Exceptions and lower agreement. Detachment, compared with the starting-pool subfactor from which it was formed, correlated .98, and Mania .77, its lower agreement reflecting the starting-pool Mania subfactor’s inclusion of items on heightened sexual interest, none of which were retained. The neurocognitive domains (median .85) and personality facets (median .87) show lower agreement because their benchmarks comprise only the items Forbes et al. recorded against each domain or facet, so the comparison is between two operationalisations of the construct rather than between a subset of items and the whole.

sections.title: MAPsy Reliability
sections.text:
Internal consistency is high at every level: every spectrum, subspectrum, neurocognitive domain, and neurocognitive disorder scale has an omega of at least .81, and the median omega exceeds .85 at every level.
Internal consistency estimates. McDonald’s omega was estimated for every construct with two or more items, with Cronbach’s alpha alongside, in the reference sample (per-construct n from 4,840 to 5,827). Median omega is .93 for the nine spectra (range .81 to .97), .94 for the two subspectra (.93 to .95), .87 for the 19 subfactors with two or more items (.76 to .96), .88 for the 31 such clusters (.80 to .95), .87 for the 20 such personality facets (.80 to .95), .87 for the six neurocognitive domains (.84 to .92), .92 for the 24 disorder scales scored from clusters (.80 to .96), .89 for the seven personality disorder scales (.59 to .94), and .95 for the two neurocognitive disorder scales, which share the same items. Median alpha is lower at every level, from .71 for the facets to .94 for the neurocognitive disorder scales, as expected where item loadings are unequal. The lowest value is that of Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features (omega = .59), whose items combine eight facets scored in the forward direction with two scored in reverse; in the reference sample the reverse-scored Anxiousness and Withdrawal items correlate negatively with the other items of the scale, so its items do not share a single dominant dimension and omega, which assumes one, is correspondingly low.
Single-item constructs. Sixty-four of the 95 clusters, two subfactors (Antisocial Behaviour and Dysregulated Eating), and three personality facets (Attention seeking, Perseveration, and Rigid perfectionism) are measured by a single item, for which internal consistency is not defined. A single-item construct’s score is the response to that item.
Test-retest reliability. Evidence of the MAPsy’s test-retest reliability has not yet been collected.

sections.title: MAPsy Validity
sections.text: Evidence of the convergent validity of the MAPsy against other measures and of its sensitivity to change has not yet been collected.

sections.title: MAPsy Thresholds
sections.text:
The severity-band thresholds were set in two ways. For the constructs of the empirical hierarchy, the personality facets, and the neurocognitive domains, thresholds are based on clinical review of each item. For the 33 DSM-5 disorder scales, they are anchored to how common each disorder is in the general population.
Item-level thresholds. The thresholds of the constructs of the empirical hierarchy, the personality facets, and the neurocognitive domains are sums of item-level thresholds set by clinical review. Each of the 154 items was assigned a first threshold, the lowest item score indicating a level of psychopathology that is of clinical interest, and a second threshold, the lowest item score indicating a clinically significant level. The thresholds were set in three stages. First, three raters independently selected thresholds for every item. The consensus for each item was then taken as the median of the three selections, or agreed through discussion with a fourth rater where selections were widely split. Finally, the consensus thresholds were reviewed against each item’s content, considering the DSM-5 criterion the item describes, where it describes one, and the raters’ judgement of how common the experience is in everyday life. The rationale for each item’s thresholds was recorded. Items describing experiences judged common in everyday life were given higher thresholds, and items describing safety-critical or under-reported experiences, such as suicidal behaviour and antagonistic conduct, lower thresholds. The reference sample did not determine the item thresholds; the proportion of the sample at or above each threshold was consulted only as context.
Disorder scale thresholds. The thresholds for the 33 DSM-5 disorder scales were instead anchored to the prevalence of each disorder in the general population, taken from the DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2013, 2022), the National Comorbidity Survey Replication (Kessler et al., 2005), and, for disorders these do not cover, other national surveys and published epidemiological studies, using 12-month prevalence where available and point or lifetime prevalence otherwise. Summed item thresholds would have made the proportion of respondents reaching a disorder scale’s thresholds depend on the number of items describing the disorder’s criteria, from two to 53, rather than on how common the disorder is. For each scale, the Elevated threshold was set at the score at or above which the proportion of the reference sample is closest to six times the disorder’s prevalence, and the Clinically Significant threshold at the score closest to four times, the multipliers allowing for the reference sample’s enrichment for psychological distress relative to the general population.
How the multipliers were set. The multiplier of four was set from an approximate estimate of the 12-month prevalence of Major Depressive Disorder in the reference sample: the proportion of the sample receiving treatment and the proportion reporting very high distress on the K10, combined with approximate rates of the disorder reported for such groups, indicate a prevalence of about 25 to 35 percent, roughly four times the general-population anchor of 8 percent. The multiplier of six was set relative to it so that the Elevated band captures an additional group of respondents about half the size of the group in the Clinically Significant band, comprising those whose symptoms of the disorder are of clinical interest.

sections.title: Why administer the MAPsy when measures of specific disorders are available?
sections.text: Because the two differ in scope. The MAPsy is broad in scope. In one administration it assesses symptoms of DSM-5 disorders on 33 disorder scales and across nine broad dimensions of psychopathology, which helps the clinician establish what needs to be assessed further. This includes disorders that are often identified only after a long delay. The MAPsy does not replace the clinical interview and disorder-specific assessment; it helps guide them.

sections.title: Why does the MAPsy report both DSM-5 disorder scales and dimensions of psychopathology?
sections.text:
The two frameworks answer different questions. The DSM-5 disorder scales serve clinical practice directly: diagnosis in mental health settings is typically made in DSM terms, clinicians are trained in its categories, and the research on assessment and treatment is organised by them. The empirical hierarchy addresses recognised limitations of categorical diagnosis, which imposes boundaries on symptoms that vary continuously (Kotov et al., 2017).
Take, for example, the co-occurrence of depressive and anxious symptoms. In the hierarchy, it is represented as a shared position on a broader spectrum, in this case Internalising. Each level, from broad spectra down to narrow symptom clusters, describes the client’s presentation at a different level of specificity (Kotov et al., 2017; Forbes et al., 2025).
Because the items are both written in the language of DSM-5 symptoms and organised into the hierarchy, one set of responses can be scored both ways, so a clinician can read the disorder scales and see where those disorders’ symptoms sit within broader dimensions of psychopathology.

sections.title: Can the MAPsy be used to make a diagnosis?
sections.text:
No. A diagnosis can only be made by a suitably qualified mental health professional, based on a comprehensive assessment. A score on a DSM-5 disorder scale describes the level of the symptoms that the MAPsy measures for that disorder over the past year and does not establish a diagnosis. Some disorder scales measure only some of a disorder’s symptoms, and diagnostic criteria also involve duration, onset, impairment, and the exclusion of other explanations (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), which a self-report symptom measure cannot assess.
A Clinically Significant disorder scale is best read as a signal that the disorder warrants further assessment, for example through a clinical interview against the criteria. Expanding the scale in the report shows which symptoms contributed to the elevation and can help guide further assessment.

sections.title: Why are the percentiles based on a mental health sample rather than the general community?
sections.text:
The reference sample was recruited for research on mental health; most of its members were receiving treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. This composition suits the measure’s purpose. A measure used to decide whether a presentation warrants further assessment needs to discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, and a sample in which high levels of distress are common represents that range more fully than a general community sample, in which most respondents score near the floor and few score in the range where clinical decisions are made.
This means a percentile compares the client with people who may have been experiencing mental health difficulties, rather than with the general population. A percentile around 50 means a typical level of psychopathology for that group, not an average level for the community.
This is why the severity bands, which are fixed to the score and do not change with the reference sample selected, carry the judgement of whether a level of psychopathology is of clinical interest or clinically significant. The percentile shows where the client sits among people who were, for the most part, receiving mental health treatment.

sections.title: Why can a subfactor or cluster be elevated when the spectrum above it is not?
sections.text:
Because a spectrum summarises a whole domain, while a subfactor or cluster captures one part of it. A client whose difficulties are focused on one area within a spectrum, such as social anxiety or sleep, can therefore be elevated on the subfactor or cluster that captures that area of difficulty while the spectrum as a whole remains Not Elevated.
This follows from how the thresholds are set. For the constructs of the hierarchy, a construct’s thresholds are the sums of its items’ thresholds, so a broad construct with many items needs more of its items at or above threshold before its score reaches the Elevated or Clinically Significant band than a narrow construct with few items does. This is by design: for a spectrum’s score to reach the Elevated or Clinically Significant band, the client must report symptoms at threshold level across a substantial share of the spectrum’s content, which is what an elevation on a broad dimension of psychopathology means. The hierarchy therefore registers severity at the level at which it is present, narrow problems on clusters and pervasive difficulties on subfactors and spectra.
The report and the interpretive text allow for this: every construct’s band is shown in the Empirical Hierarchy panel, and the interpretive text names elevated subfactors even when their spectrum is not elevated.

sections.title: How do the personality facets relate to the PID-5-SF?
sections.text: The MAPsy’s 23 personality facets carry the same names as facets of the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 – Short Form (PID-5-SF), because both follow the trait facets of the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders, but they are not scored from the same items, and they serve a different purpose. The PID-5-SF gives a trait profile; in the MAPsy the facets are the building blocks of the seven personality disorder scales, and they appear in the report within those scales rather than as a profile of their own.

sections.title: Why does the Harmful Substance Use spectrum sometimes show no score?
sections.text: Because it is scored only for clients who report using a substance in the past year. Part-way through the questionnaire, the client is asked which substances they have used in the past year, from a checklist of seven classes. A client who selects one or more is then asked nine further items about substance use disorder symptoms and use in dangerous situations, and the Harmful Substance Use spectrum is scored from those items. A client who selects “None of the above” is not asked these items, so the spectrum and its clusters are shown in the report without a score, and the three checklist clusters (Alcohol use, Cannabis use, and Illicit and prescription substance use) are marked No.

sourceGuidance.title: MAPsy Scoring
sourceGuidance.text:
The MAPsy yields scores for nine spectra, two subspectra, 21 subfactors, and 95 clusters of the empirical hierarchy, and for 23 personality facets, six neurocognitive domains, and 33 DSM-5 disorder scales. A construct’s score is the sum of its constituent item scores. Higher scores indicate that the construct’s items were rated as more true, or more common, over the past year.
The score itself is not displayed in the report: it is converted to a percentile and assigned a severity band, and the report presents those.
For the Antisocial Personality Disorder with Psychopathic Features scale, the items measuring Anxiousness and Withdrawal are reverse scored before summing, so that low anxiousness and low withdrawal contribute to the scale in the direction that defines the disorder.

sourceGuidance.title: MAPsy Percentiles
sourceGuidance.text:
Percentiles are the primary metric for presenting scores because they are comparable across constructs, regardless of the number of items, and are readily communicated to clients and other professionals. Each score is converted to a percentile against the distribution of scores on that construct in a reference sample drawn from Forbes et al.’s (2025) study. Percentiles can be based on the whole reference sample, All (respondents aged 16 years and over), or on one of two subsets of it, Youth (16 to 24 years) and Adult (25 years and over). The Youth or Adult sample is selected by default from the client’s age at administration, calculated from their date of birth, and the Adult sample is used when no date of birth is entered.
The reference sample is best described as a distress-enriched sample: most of its members were receiving mental health treatment and more than half reported very high psychological distress. Percentiles therefore describe the client’s standing relative to that population rather than the general community. A score at the 50th percentile is typical of that population and does not indicate an average level of psychopathology relative to the general community. A distress-enriched sample has the advantage that its percentiles discriminate among individuals across the full range of severity, including the high levels seen in clinical settings.
The percentile does not itself say whether a level of psychopathology is clinically significant; that judgement is carried by the severity band. The percentile instead shows how far the client’s level of psychopathology is from what is typical of the reference sample.

sections.title: PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5)
sections.text:
The Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) is a 20-item self-report measure of the twenty DSM-5 symptoms of PTSD in adult populations (ages 18+). It is designed for use with people who have experienced traumatic events.
3 minutes
Ages 18+
Diagnosis , Trauma

sections.title: Psychiatric Clinical Interview and Assessment (Assessment Session)
sections.text: Read full video transcript ⇲

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
As clinicians, we see it all the time. A client comes in complaining of insomnia, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. You might suspect depression, anxiety, or stress. But what if it’s trauma—and no one has ever asked?
PTSD is one of the most commonly under-identified conditions in adult mental health care. And when I say under-identified, I mean systematically missed—even when patients are sitting right in front of us showing every symptom.
In fact, a 2018 systematic review found that when mental health patients were screened for PTSD, about one in three met the diagnostic criteria. Yet only about one in ten of those cases were already documented in clinical records.
So why does this keep happening? The uncomfortable truth is that we’re not asking. Patients may not volunteer trauma experiences because they don’t connect their current symptoms with past trauma. In addition, avoidance itself is a symptom of PTSD, which may prevent people from talking about it. As a result, trauma often stays hidden.

sections.title: Why PTSD Is Often Missed
sections.text:
Flashbacks can easily be mistaken for hallucinations. Avoidance may appear as depression. Hypervigilance can look like anxiety.
Trauma rarely walks into the clinic clearly labelled as PTSD. Instead, it shows up wearing other diagnoses. Patients can cycle through treatments that don’t work because clinicians are treating the wrong condition. Without routine trauma screening built into treatment protocols, these patterns often remain invisible.
I’m Dr. Hilah Kaufman, and today we’re taking a closer look at the PCL-5—a brief, validated tool that can help identify trauma that may have been there all along.

sections.title: What the PCL-5 Is
sections.text:
The PTSD Checklist for DSM-5, or PCL-5, is a 20-item self-report questionnaire designed to assess PTSD symptoms in adults who have experienced trauma.
Developed by the VA’s National Center for PTSD, it is well validated, widely used, and free. Different versions are available depending on clinical needs.
Each item corresponds directly to one of the 20 DSM-5 PTSD criteria, and each is rated on a 0 to 4 scale based on symptoms experienced over the past month. This produces a total score ranging from 0 to 80.
What makes the PCL-5 especially useful clinically is how the 20 items map onto the four DSM-5 symptom clusters for PTSD: re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal. This structure helps clinicians see which symptoms are driving the distress.

sections.title: Example Case
sections.text:
Let’s look at an example.
Michael is a 24-year-old who came to therapy complaining of poor sleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. He didn’t mention trauma.
His total score was 32, just below the commonly used cutoff of 33.
Then we examine the symptom clusters—and this is where the picture changes.
For Michael, avoidance was severe and re-experiencing was moderate. His negative cognitions and mood, as well as arousal symptoms, were both in the normal range.
This pattern doesn’t reflect generalized distress. It reflects a trauma-specific pattern driven by avoidance. And that distinction matters clinically. Even though Michael’s total score fell just below the cutoff, his responses met the DSM-5 symptom cluster criteria, supporting a provisional PTSD diagnosis.
Only later did Michael disclose the trauma itself: a serious car accident he experienced as a child that he had been actively avoiding thinking or talking about.

sections.title: Using the PCL-5 in Treatment
sections.text:
This illustrates the power of the PCL-5. It helps clinicians screen for PTSD, identify symptom patterns, support diagnosis, and monitor change over time.
When results suggest PTSD, that’s not the end of the process—it’s just the beginning. Clinicians should always confirm findings with further clinical assessment and then move toward trauma-focused, evidence-based care.
After six months of trauma-focused therapy, Michael’s total score dropped significantly. Research suggests that a 12-point change represents clinically meaningful improvement, allowing clinicians to track whether treatment is working.

sections.title: Important Considerations
sections.text:
There are a few important things to keep in mind when using the PCL-5.
First, it is a screening tool that can support a provisional diagnosis, but it does not replace clinical judgement. Second, it is self-report, meaning responses depend on the client’s mood and willingness to disclose. Third, it reflects a 30-day snapshot, not the person’s entire clinical history.
Finally, it should not be administered blindly. Pair it with a trauma exposure screener, or ensure trauma exposure has already been established.
The PCL-5 is a powerful tool, but it should never be used in isolation.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text:
Trauma rarely announces itself when patients walk through the door. Clinicians need structured ways to identify it.
The PCL-5 provides a systematic way to detect trauma that might otherwise remain hidden. It doesn’t replace clinical judgement—it sharpens it.
Somewhere in your caseload right now is undiagnosed trauma. The PCL-5 helps you find it.

sections.title: PCL-5 Overview
sections.text:
Consistent with the DSM-5, the four symptom clusters are represented in the PCL-5 by the following subscales:
1. Re-experiencing (Criterion B) : This subscale measures the persistent re-experiencing of the traumatic event(s) through intrusive thoughts, nightmares, flashbacks, or distressing memories. Individuals may feel as if the traumatic event is recurring, leading to significant psychological distress. Re-experiencing symptoms can be triggered by internal or external cues related to the traumatic event.
2. Avoidance (Criterion C) : This subscale assesses efforts to avoid thoughts, feelings, or reminders associated with the traumatic event. Avoidance behaviours may include avoiding places, people, activities, or conversations that remind the individual of the trauma. Avoidance serves as a coping mechanism to reduce distress but can interfere with the individual’s ability to process and heal from the trauma.
3. Negative Alterations in Cognition and Mood (Criterion D) : This subscale measures the negative impact on thoughts and feelings that began or worsened after the traumatic event. Symptoms may include persistent negative beliefs about oneself, others, or the world; distorted blame of oneself or others for causing the traumatic event; persistent negative emotions such as fear, anger, guilt, or shame; diminished interest in activities once enjoyed; feeling detached from others; and an inability to experience positive emotions.
4. Hyperarousal (Criterion E) : This subscale measures heightened arousal and reactivity that may present as difficulty sleeping, irritability, angry outbursts, difficulty concentrating, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle response. Individuals with hyperarousal symptoms may feel constantly on edge, as if they are in a state of heightened alertness or danger.

sections.title: Example PCL-5 items:
sections.text: The PCL-5 is widely used in clinical and research settings to screen for PTSD, assess symptom severity, and monitor treatment progress over time (Forkus et al., 2023).

sections.title: Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
Total scores can range from 0 to 80, with higher scores indicating greater PTSD symptom severity. Percentiles are also presented for the total score in comparison to both a normative and clinical (PTSD) sample. A normative percentile of 50 is indicative of an average score for someone who does not have PTSD, whereas a PTSD percentile of 50 is indicative of an average score for someone who is currently in care for PTSD.
There are four subscales which match the four symptom clusters for PTSD within DSM-5:
1. Re-experiencing (criterion B, items 1-5, max score = 20)
2. Avoidance (criterion C, items 6-7, max score = 8)
3. Negative alterations in cognition and mood (Criterion D, items 8-14, max score = 28)
4. Hyper-arousal (Criterion E, items 15-20, max score = 24)
In addition to a raw score being presented, a mean score is also computed, which is the subscale score divided by the number of items within that subscale. The average score can help determine elevated symptom clusters when comparing each of the four subscales. These scores range between 0 to 4, where higher scores represent higher severity. Consistent with the likert scale:
0 = Not at all
1 = A little bit
2 = Moderately
3 = Quite a bit
4 = Extremely
Symptom descriptors are also presented for the total score and each of the subscale scores. These descriptors are determined by the distance from the normative mean:
Normal Range – Average score less than or equal to 1.23
Mild – Average score above 1.23 and less than or equal to 1.64
Moderate – Average score above 1.64 and less than or equal to 2.455
Severe – Average score above 2.455 and less than or equal to 3.265
Extremely Severe – Average score above 3.265
Given the PCL-5 questions closely reassembled the diagnostic criteria in the DSM-5-TR, a provisional PTSD diagnosis can be made based on the following rule. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria requires at least: 1 Criterion B item (questions 1-5), 1 Criterion C item (questions 6-7), 2 Criterion D items (questions 8-14), and 2 Criterion E items (questions 15-20). A score of 2 (Moderately on the likert scale ) or higher is an endorsed symptom.
Notwithstanding the DSM related diagnostic criteria, scores of 33 or above are considered to be of clinical significance, and can serve as an alternative threshold for identifying significant PTSD symptoms that interfere with daily functioning (Bovin et al., 2016; Krüger-Gottschalk et al., 2017; Rosendahl et al., 2019).
A comparison graph is presented showing where the respondent’s score sits in comparison to the normative and PTSD samples, with shaded areas around the means indicating the two middle quartiles (between 25th and 75th percentile). This graph can help contextualise PCL-5 total scores in comparison to the distribution of responses among clinical and non-clinical groups. A cutoff score of 33 indicates the point at which symptoms are defined as clinically significant.

sections.title: Psychometric Properties
sections.text:
A review of the PCL-5 using 51 studies demonstrated that the internal consistency for the total score ranged between .83 – .97 (Forkus et al., 2023). Test-retest reliability was tested across a range of time intervals and was found to range between .58 – .91 (Forkus et al., 2023). The PCL–5 total score showed moderate to strong correlations with other measures of PTSD (.44–.89; Forkus et al., 2023). Construct validity was assessed using group difference tests. Individuals with PTSD (vs. without PTSD) had a significantly higher PCL–5 total score (Fung et al., 2019) and individuals with probable PTSD (determined using recommended cutoff scores) had significantly greater mental functional impairment compared with those without probable PTSD (Forkus et al., 2023).
The normative percentiles are calculated from a combination of a non-clinical, non-trauma exposed group and a non-clinical but some trauma exposed group (N = 166, M = 16.47, SD = 16.29; Renyer, 2016). This group was combined to provide a more realistic non-clinical group where some of the group may have experienced some trauma (but not have PTSD) and some of the group have not experienced any trauma at all. Renyer (2016) also determined a reliable change score of 12. The clinical (PTSD) percentiles are calculated from a sample of military veterans in clinical care for PTSD (N = 468, M = 36.97, SD = 21.16; Bovin et al., 2016).
The distance from the normative mean described above was used to produce symptom descriptors:
Normal Range – < 0.5 SD below mean (average score less than or equal to 1.23)
Mild – 0.5 to 1 SD above mean (average score above 1.23 and less than or equal to 1.64)
Moderate – 1 to 2 SD above mean (average score above 1.64 and less than or equal to 2.455)
Severe – 2 to 3 SD above mean (average score above 2.455 and less than or equal to 3.265)
Extremely Severe – > 3 SD above mean (average score above 3.265)

sections.title: PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5)
sections.text:
The Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) is a 20-item self-report measure of the twenty DSM-5 symptoms of PTSD in adult populations (ages 18+). It is designed for use with people who have experienced traumatic events.
3 minutes
Ages 18+
Diagnosis , Trauma

sections.title: PCL-5 Overview
sections.text:
Consistent with the DSM-5, the four symptom clusters are represented in the PCL-5 by the following subscales:
1. Re-experiencing (Criterion B) : This subscale measures the persistent re-experiencing of the traumatic event(s) through intrusive thoughts, nightmares, flashbacks, or distressing memories. Individuals may feel as if the traumatic event is recurring, leading to significant psychological distress. Re-experiencing symptoms can be triggered by internal or external cues related to the traumatic event.
2. Avoidance (Criterion C) : This subscale assesses efforts to avoid thoughts, feelings, or reminders associated with the traumatic event. Avoidance behaviours may include avoiding places, people, activities, or conversations that remind the individual of the trauma. Avoidance serves as a coping mechanism to reduce distress but can interfere with the individual’s ability to process and heal from the trauma.
3. Negative Alterations in Cognition and Mood (Criterion D) : This subscale measures the negative impact on thoughts and feelings that began or worsened after the traumatic event. Symptoms may include persistent negative beliefs about oneself, others, or the world; distorted blame of oneself or others for causing the traumatic event; persistent negative emotions such as fear, anger, guilt, or shame; diminished interest in activities once enjoyed; feeling detached from others; and an inability to experience positive emotions.
4. Hyperarousal (Criterion E) : This subscale measures heightened arousal and reactivity that may present as difficulty sleeping, irritability, angry outbursts, difficulty concentrating, hypervigilance, and an exaggerated startle response. Individuals with hyperarousal symptoms may feel constantly on edge, as if they are in a state of heightened alertness or danger.

sections.text: The PCL-5 is widely used in clinical and research settings to screen for PTSD, assess symptom severity, and monitor treatment progress over time (Forkus et al., 2023).

sections.title: Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
Total scores can range from 0 to 80, with higher scores indicating greater PTSD symptom severity. Percentiles are also presented for the total score in comparison to both a normative and clinical (PTSD) sample. A normative percentile of 50 is indicative of an average score for someone who does not have PTSD, whereas a PTSD percentile of 50 is indicative of an average score for someone who is currently in care for PTSD.
There are four subscales which match the four symptom clusters for PTSD within DSM-5:
1. Re-experiencing (criterion B, items 1-5, max score = 20)
2. Avoidance (criterion C, items 6-7, max score = 8)
3. Negative alterations in cognition and mood (Criterion D, items 8-14, max score = 28)
4. Hyper-arousal (Criterion E, items 15-20, max score = 24)
In addition to a raw score being presented, a mean score is also computed, which is the subscale score divided by the number of items within that subscale. The average score can help determine elevated symptom clusters when comparing each of the four subscales. These scores range between 0 to 4, where higher scores represent higher severity. Consistent with the likert scale:
0 = Not at all
1 = A little bit
2 = Moderately
3 = Quite a bit
4 = Extremely
Symptom descriptors are also presented for the total score and each of the subscale scores. These descriptors are determined by the distance from the normative mean:
Normal Range – Average score less than or equal to 1.23
Mild – Average score above 1.23 and less than or equal to 1.64
Moderate – Average score above 1.64 and less than or equal to 2.455
Severe – Average score above 2.455 and less than or equal to 3.265
Extremely Severe – Average score above 3.265
Given the PCL-5 questions closely reassembled the diagnostic criteria in the DSM-5-TR, a provisional PTSD diagnosis can be made based on the following rule. The DSM-5 diagnostic criteria requires at least: 1 Criterion B item (questions 1-5), 1 Criterion C item (questions 6-7), 2 Criterion D items (questions 8-14), and 2 Criterion E items (questions 15-20). A score of 2 (Moderately on the likert scale ) or higher is an endorsed symptom.
Notwithstanding the DSM related diagnostic criteria, scores of 33 or above are considered to be of clinical significance, and can serve as an alternative threshold for identifying significant PTSD symptoms that interfere with daily functioning (Bovin et al., 2016; Krüger-Gottschalk et al., 2017; Rosendahl et al., 2019).
A comparison graph is presented showing where the respondent’s score sits in comparison to the normative and PTSD samples, with shaded areas around the means indicating the two middle quartiles (between 25th and 75th percentile). This graph can help contextualise PCL-5 total scores in comparison to the distribution of responses among clinical and non-clinical groups. A cutoff score of 33 indicates the point at which symptoms are defined as clinically significant.
When administered more than once, longitudinal graphs are presented showing change in symptoms over time. A 12 point change during the course of treatment represents clinically significant change (Renyer, 2016).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
As clinicians, we see it all the time. A client comes in complaining of insomnia, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. You might suspect depression, anxiety, or stress. But what if it’s trauma—and no one has ever asked?
PTSD is one of the most commonly under-identified conditions in adult mental health care. And when I say under-identified, I mean systematically missed—even when patients are sitting right in front of us showing every symptom.
In fact, a 2018 systematic review found that when mental health patients were screened for PTSD, about one in three met the diagnostic criteria. Yet only about one in ten of those cases were already documented in clinical records.
So why does this keep happening? The uncomfortable truth is that we’re not asking. Patients may not volunteer trauma experiences because they don’t connect their current symptoms with past trauma. In addition, avoidance itself is a symptom of PTSD, which may prevent people from talking about it. As a result, trauma often stays hidden.

sections.title: Why PTSD Is Often Missed
sections.text:
Flashbacks can easily be mistaken for hallucinations. Avoidance may appear as depression. Hypervigilance can look like anxiety.
Trauma rarely walks into the clinic clearly labelled as PTSD. Instead, it shows up wearing other diagnoses. Patients can cycle through treatments that don’t work because clinicians are treating the wrong condition. Without routine trauma screening built into treatment protocols, these patterns often remain invisible.
I’m Dr. Hilah Kaufman, and today we’re taking a closer look at the PCL-5—a brief, validated tool that can help identify trauma that may have been there all along.

sections.title: What the PCL-5 Is
sections.text:
The PTSD Checklist for DSM-5, or PCL-5, is a 20-item self-report questionnaire designed to assess PTSD symptoms in adults who have experienced trauma.
Developed by the VA’s National Center for PTSD, it is well validated, widely used, and free. Different versions are available depending on clinical needs.
Each item corresponds directly to one of the 20 DSM-5 PTSD criteria, and each is rated on a 0 to 4 scale based on symptoms experienced over the past month. This produces a total score ranging from 0 to 80.
What makes the PCL-5 especially useful clinically is how the 20 items map onto the four DSM-5 symptom clusters for PTSD: re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal. This structure helps clinicians see which symptoms are driving the distress.

sections.title: Example Case
sections.text:
Let’s look at an example.
Michael is a 24-year-old who came to therapy complaining of poor sleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. He didn’t mention trauma.
His total score was 32, just below the commonly used cutoff of 33.
Then we examine the symptom clusters—and this is where the picture changes.
For Michael, avoidance was severe and re-experiencing was moderate. His negative cognitions and mood, as well as arousal symptoms, were both in the normal range.
This pattern doesn’t reflect generalized distress. It reflects a trauma-specific pattern driven by avoidance. And that distinction matters clinically. Even though Michael’s total score fell just below the cutoff, his responses met the DSM-5 symptom cluster criteria, supporting a provisional PTSD diagnosis.
Only later did Michael disclose the trauma itself: a serious car accident he experienced as a child that he had been actively avoiding thinking or talking about.

sections.title: Using the PCL-5 in Treatment
sections.text:
This illustrates the power of the PCL-5. It helps clinicians screen for PTSD, identify symptom patterns, support diagnosis, and monitor change over time.
When results suggest PTSD, that’s not the end of the process—it’s just the beginning. Clinicians should always confirm findings with further clinical assessment and then move toward trauma-focused, evidence-based care.
After six months of trauma-focused therapy, Michael’s total score dropped significantly. Research suggests that a 12-point change represents clinically meaningful improvement, allowing clinicians to track whether treatment is working.

sections.title: Important Considerations
sections.text:
There are a few important things to keep in mind when using the PCL-5.
First, it is a screening tool that can support a provisional diagnosis, but it does not replace clinical judgement. Second, it is self-report, meaning responses depend on the client’s mood and willingness to disclose. Third, it reflects a 30-day snapshot, not the person’s entire clinical history.
Finally, it should not be administered blindly. Pair it with a trauma exposure screener, or ensure trauma exposure has already been established.
The PCL-5 is a powerful tool, but it should never be used in isolation.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text:
Trauma rarely announces itself when patients walk through the door. Clinicians need structured ways to identify it.
The PCL-5 provides a systematic way to detect trauma that might otherwise remain hidden. It doesn’t replace clinical judgement—it sharpens it.
Somewhere in your caseload right now is undiagnosed trauma. The PCL-5 helps you find it.

sections.title: GAD-7 Overview
sections.text:
GAD is a mental health condition characterised by persistent and excessive worry about various aspects of daily life (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The GAD-7 assessment asks patients to evaluate their level of symptoms over the last two weeks. When administered on multiple occasions at the start, middle, and end of treatment, responses can be used to track treatment progress over time.
Given the simple language used in the assessment, it is appropriate for individuals as young as 14 years. When used as a screening tool, a score of 10 or greater is associated with Generalised Anxiety Disorder (Sensitivity 89% and Specificity 82%) (Spitzer et al., 2006). However, the GAD-7 is sensitive to anxiety symptoms in general, with scores over 10 also related to other disorders such as panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Kroenke, et al. 2007).

sections.title: GAD-7 Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
A raw score (from 0 to 21) is presented as well as a percentile rank based on a normative community sample (Stocker et al., 2021) of age-related peers. A higher score indicates higher levels of anxiety symptoms.
Percentiles are calculated according to the age of the client and provide a useful context for comparing a respondent’s results with levels of anxiety seen in the community. A percentile of 50 represents typical and relatively healthy patterns of anxiety, falling within the mild range of anxiety for younger age groups (50 years of age or less).
Experiencing at least some anxiety is relatively normal, particularly among younger age groups. Approximately 11% of individuals under 30 fall into the “severe” anxiety range, whereas 1.4% of people over 70 years of age have scores in that range. Given that experiencing anxiety is common, anxiety is best considered on a dimensional basis (e.g. the degree to which someone has symptoms) rather than in a binary absent/present fashion.
The scale classifies individuals into distinct severity categories based on their raw scores, as follows:
None-Minimal (Scores of 4 or below): Scores within this range suggest minimal anxiety, with symptoms being either absent or so slight that they have little to no impact on daily functioning.
Mild (Scores between 5 and 9): Anxiety is present and noticeable but generally manageable, with only occasional interference in daily activities.
Moderate (Scores between 10 and 14): Anxiety symptoms are frequent and intense, potentially affecting the individual’s ability to perform daily tasks effectively. They are more likely than not to have a diagnosable anxiety disorder such as generalised anxiety disorder.
Severe (Scores of 15 and above): Anxiety symptoms are intense and persistent, significantly disrupting daily functioning. They likely have a diagnosable anxiety disorder or other psychiatric condition.
When administered multiple times, the total scores are graphed over time.
A significant change in score is defined as an increase or decrease of at least 6 points. This criterion is based on the Reliable Change Index (Bischoff et al., 2020). Such changes indicate significant change symptoms, while a change of less than the specified points indicates minimal change in symptom severity between assessments.
Scores of 10 or greater are indicative of Generalised Anxiety Disorder (Sensitivity 89% and Specificity 82%) (Spitzer et al., 2006) and other psychiatric disorders involving anxiety. Scores of 10 or more may also indicate panic disorder (sensitivity 74%, specificity 81%), social anxiety disorder (sensitivity 72%, specificity 80%), and post-traumatic stress disorder (sensitivity 66%, specificity 81%) (Kroenke, et al. 2007).
Higher scores on the GAD-7 indicate the presence of anxiety symptoms, however 90% of individuals with GAD experience at least one additional psychiatric condition over their lifetime. While major depressive disorder (MDD) is the most prevalent comorbidity among individuals with GAD, dysthymia, bipolar, alcohol abuse are also frequently observed (Simon, 2009; Preti et al., 2015).

sections.title: GAD-7 Psychometric Properties
sections.text:
Lowe et al. (2008) investigated the validity and reliability of the GAD-7. The normative community sample consisted of a total of 5,036 individuals, with an average age of 48.4 years ( SD = 18) and 53.6% of participants being women. Confirmatory factor analyses substantiated the 1-dimensional structure of the GAD-7. Internal consistency was identical across all subgroups (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89). Intercorrelations with the PHQ-2 and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale were r = 0.64 ( p < 0.001) and r = -0.43 ( p < 0.001), respectively. Women had significantly higher mean ( SD ) GAD-7 anxiety scores compared with men [3.2 (3.5) vs. 2.7 (3.2); p < 0.001]. Approximately 5% of subjects had GAD-7 scores of 10 or greater, and 1% had GAD-7 scores of 15 or greater.
The GAD-7 has consistently demonstrated robust psychometric properties across various samples. It has been validated in primary care settings (Spitzer et al., 2006) and population-based samples (Löwe et al., 2008). Recent research aimed to further evaluate its effectiveness in clinical settings. A study by Rutters and Brown (2017) involved 536 patients from the Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders (CARD) at Boston University, with participants averaging 31.49 years of age ( SD = 12.05; 62.7% female) and ranging from 18 to 80 years. The study reaffirmed the GAD-7’s unidimensional structure, as a one-factor model fit the clinical data well. The scale exhibited strong reliability with a coefficient of .85 for the full sample and when analysed by gender. Additionally, the GAD-7 demonstrated good convergent validity, showing higher correlations with other anxiety measures, such as the Depression Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS) – Anxiety ( r = .58), DASS – Stress ( r = .68), and Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ) ( r = .66), compared to measures of depression like DASS – Depression ( r = .48) and Obsessive Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCD-R) ( r = .42).
Normative community percentiles were derived through interpolation using data from an Australian sample of 13,829 individuals, with 75.5% of the participants identifying as female (Stocker et al., 2021). The norms were stratified by age groups as follows:
Ages 18-29: Mean = 7.8, SD = 5.9
Ages 30-49: Mean = 6.6, SD = 5.4
Ages 50-69: Mean = 4.6, SD = 4.9
Age 70+: Mean = 2.6, SD = 3.6

sections.title: GAD-7 Overview
sections.text:
GAD is a mental health condition characterised by persistent and excessive worry about various aspects of daily life (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The GAD-7 assessment asks patients to evaluate their level of symptoms over the last two weeks. When administered on multiple occasions at the start, middle, and end of treatment, responses can be used to track treatment progress over time.
Given the simple language used in the assessment, it is appropriate for individuals as young as 14 years. When used as a screening tool, a score of 10 or greater is associated with Generalised Anxiety Disorder (Sensitivity 89% and Specificity 82%) (Spitzer et al., 2006). However, the GAD-7 is sensitive to anxiety symptoms in general, with scores over 10 also related to other disorders such as panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Kroenke, et al. 2007).

sections.title: GAD-7 Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
A raw score (from 0 to 21) is presented as well as a percentile rank based on a normative community sample (Stocker et al., 2021) of age-related peers. A higher score indicates higher levels of anxiety symptoms.
Percentiles are calculated according to the age of the client and provide a useful context for comparing a respondent’s results with levels of anxiety seen in the community. A percentile of 50 represents typical and relatively healthy patterns of anxiety, falling within the mild range of anxiety for younger age groups (50 years of age or less).
Experiencing at least some anxiety is relatively normal, particularly among younger age groups. Approximately 11% of individuals under 30 fall into the “severe” anxiety range, whereas 1.4% of people over 70 years of age have scores in that range. Given that experiencing anxiety is common, anxiety is best considered on a dimensional basis (e.g. the degree to which someone has symptoms) rather than in a binary absent/present fashion.
The scale classifies individuals into distinct severity categories based on their raw scores, as follows:
None-Minimal (Scores of 4 or below): Scores within this range suggest minimal anxiety, with symptoms being either absent or so slight that they have little to no impact on daily functioning.
Mild (Scores between 5 and 9): Anxiety is present and noticeable but generally manageable, with only occasional interference in daily activities.
Moderate (Scores between 10 and 14): Anxiety symptoms are frequent and intense, potentially affecting the individual’s ability to perform daily tasks effectively. They are more likely than not to have a diagnosable anxiety disorder such as generalised anxiety disorder.
Severe (Scores of 15 and above): Anxiety symptoms are intense and persistent, significantly disrupting daily functioning. They likely have a diagnosable anxiety disorder or other psychiatric condition.
When administered multiple times, the total scores are graphed over time.
A significant change in score is defined as an increase or decrease of at least 6 points. This criterion is based on the Reliable Change Index (Bischoff et al., 2020). Such changes indicate significant change symptoms, while a change of less than the specified points indicates minimal change in symptom severity between assessments.
Scores of 10 or greater are indicative of Generalised Anxiety Disorder (Sensitivity 89% and Specificity 82%) (Spitzer et al., 2006) and other psychiatric disorders involving anxiety. Scores of 10 or more may also indicate panic disorder (sensitivity 74%, specificity 81%), social anxiety disorder (sensitivity 72%, specificity 80%), and post-traumatic stress disorder (sensitivity 66%, specificity 81%) (Kroenke, et al. 2007).
Higher scores on the GAD-7 indicate the presence of anxiety symptoms, however 90% of individuals with GAD experience at least one additional psychiatric condition over their lifetime. While major depressive disorder (MDD) is the most prevalent comorbidity among individuals with GAD, dysthymia, bipolar, alcohol abuse are also frequently observed (Simon, 2009; Preti et al., 2015).

sections.title: GAD-7 Psychometric Properties
sections.text:
Lowe et al. (2008) investigated the validity and reliability of the GAD-7. The normative community sample consisted of a total of 5,036 individuals, with an average age of 48.4 years ( SD = 18) and 53.6% of participants being women. Confirmatory factor analyses substantiated the 1-dimensional structure of the GAD-7. Internal consistency was identical across all subgroups (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.89). Intercorrelations with the PHQ-2 and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale were r = 0.64 ( p < 0.001) and r = -0.43 ( p < 0.001), respectively. Women had significantly higher mean ( SD ) GAD-7 anxiety scores compared with men [3.2 (3.5) vs. 2.7 (3.2); p < 0.001]. Approximately 5% of subjects had GAD-7 scores of 10 or greater, and 1% had GAD-7 scores of 15 or greater.
The GAD-7 has consistently demonstrated robust psychometric properties across various samples. It has been validated in primary care settings (Spitzer et al., 2006) and population-based samples (Löwe et al., 2008). Recent research aimed to further evaluate its effectiveness in clinical settings. A study by Rutters and Brown (2017) involved 536 patients from the Center for Anxiety and Related Disorders (CARD) at Boston University, with participants averaging 31.49 years of age ( SD = 12.05; 62.7% female) and ranging from 18 to 80 years. The study reaffirmed the GAD-7’s unidimensional structure, as a one-factor model fit the clinical data well. The scale exhibited strong reliability with a coefficient of .85 for the full sample and when analysed by gender. Additionally, the GAD-7 demonstrated good convergent validity, showing higher correlations with other anxiety measures, such as the Depression Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS) – Anxiety ( r = .58), DASS – Stress ( r = .68), and Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ) ( r = .66), compared to measures of depression like DASS – Depression ( r = .48) and Obsessive Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCD-R) ( r = .42).
Normative community percentiles were derived through interpolation using data from an Australian sample of 13,829 individuals, with 75.5% of the participants identifying as female (Stocker et al., 2021). The norms were stratified by age groups as follows:
Ages 18-29: Mean = 7.8, SD = 5.9
Ages 30-49: Mean = 6.6, SD = 5.4
Ages 50-69: Mean = 4.6, SD = 4.9
Age 70+: Mean = 2.6, SD = 3.6

sections.text:
The following table illustrates how total scores (see Table 1) compare to the normative community sample (Stocker et al., 2021). Each score is accompanied by a corresponding normative community percentile, indicating the percentage of individuals who scored the same or lower in that age group. For example, a score of 6 corresponds to the 49th percentile for individuals under 30 in the normative community. For those aged 31 to 49, a score of 6 is at the 58th percentile. This indicates that 49% of individuals under 30 and 58% of those between 31 and 49 scored 6 or lower in the normative community sample. These graphs help contextualising an individual’s total scores on the GAD-7, providing a clearer understanding of their standing relative to other individuals in the community.

sections.title: Patient Health Questionnaire – Depression (PHQ-9)
sections.text:
The PHQ-9 is the nine item depression scale from the Patient Health Questionnaire, and is a widely used tool for assisting primary care clinicians in identifying depression as well as monitoring treatment (Kroenke et al., 2001).
2 minutes
Ages 13+
Depression , Outcome Monitoring

sections.title: PHQ-9 Overview
sections.text:
The PHQ-9 is based directly on the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) and asks about symptoms in the previous two weeks. The PHQ-9 is a widely used tool for screening, diagnosing, and monitoring depression in both clinical and non-clinical settings (Kocalevent et al., 2013). Clinically, it supports treatment planning and tracking changes in symptoms, while in non-clinical settings like schools or workplaces, it serves as an initial screening tool to identify individuals who may need further evaluation. The PHQ-9 is appropriate for individuals aged 13 years and older, making it suitable for adolescents and adults (Kroenke et al., 2001; Richardson et al., 2011).
Scores are categorised into the following ranges (Kroenke et al., 2001):
No or minimal depression: No or minor depressive symptoms that do not significantly impact daily functioning. The majority (76%) of people in the community score within this range.
Mild depression: Depressive symptoms that may cause some difficulty in daily activities.
Moderate depression: Moderate depressive symptoms that likely interfere with daily life and well-being.
Moderate-severe depression: Pronounced depressive symptoms that substantially affect daily functioning and quality of life.
Severe depression: Severe depressive symptoms that profoundly disrupt daily activities and require immediate attention.
The PHQ-9 was created to provide a quick, reliable method for evaluating the presence and severity of depressive symptoms based on the criteria outlined in the DSM. Each of its nine items corresponds to one of the symptoms of major depression, and it allows for a severity score to aid in clinical decision-making (Kroenke et al., 2001).

sections.title: PHQ-9 Scoring & Interpretation
sections.text:
A raw score (from 0 to 27) is presented where higher scores indicate more depressive symptoms.
The scale classifies individuals into distinct severity categories based on their raw scores, as follows:
No or minimal depression – Scores between 0 to 4 : Scores in this range suggest minimal depressive symptoms that do not significantly impact daily functioning. The majority (76%) of people in the community score within this range.
Mild depression – Scores between 5 to 9 : Scores in this range suggest some depressive symptoms that may cause some difficulty in daily activities. Approximately 18% of the community scores within this range.
Moderate depression – Scores between 10 to 14 : Scores in this range suggest moderate depressive symptoms that likely interfere with daily life and well-being. People who score in this range likely meet the diagnostic criteria for a depressive disorder.
Moderate-severe depression – Scores between 15 to 19 : Scores in this range suggest pronounced depressive symptoms consistent with major depressive disorder that substantially affect daily functioning and quality of life.
Severe depression – Scores between 20 to 27 : Scores in this range suggest severe depressive symptoms that profoundly disrupt daily activities and require immediate attention. Scores in this range are consistent with severe major depressive disorder.
Percentiles are calculated and provide a useful context for comparing a respondent’s results with a normative community sample. A percentile of 50 represents typical patterns of responding, while higher percentiles represent higher levels of depressive symptoms. Percentiles of 76 and below corresponding to a raw score of 4, indicate no or minimal depressive symptoms (Kocalevent et al., 2013).
The horizontal graph presents the total score in comparison to individuals from the general population, individuals with major depression and people with a depressive disorder (other than major depression). Shaded areas are presented around the two middle quartiles (between the 25th and 75th percentile) (Kroenke et al., 2001; Kocalevent et al., 2013). The major depression distribution represents individuals diagnosed with major depression. The depressive distribution represents scores from individuals who have other depressive disorder, such as dysthymic disorder or adjustment disorder with depressed mood.
Scores of 10 or more have been shown to reliably predict major depression, with a sensitivity of 81.4%, meaning that 81.4% of individuals who truly have the condition score above this point. The Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is 92.2%, indicating that when a score is 10 or more, there is a 92.2% chance the individual actually has major depression (Urtasun et al., 2019).
When using the PHQ-9 to track symptoms over time, a significant change in score is defined as an increase or decrease of 5 or more points. This criterion is based on the Reliable Change Index. Such changes indicate reliable and significant improvement or deterioration in symptoms.
Higher scores on the PHQ-9 indicate more severe depressive symptoms, which can be particularly concerning when coupled with comorbid mental disorders. Individuals with elevated PHQ-9 scores may experience intensified feelings of sadness, anxiety, or distress, making it more challenging to manage daily responsibilities and relationships (Johansson et al., 2013). This can lead to poorer life outcomes, such as increased absenteeism at work or school, greater difficulty in social interactions, and is associated with higher prevalence of substance use (Johansson et al., 2013). The PHQ-9 focuses on depressive symptoms and therefore does not detect other high prevalence disorders such as anxiety or general levels of psychological distress.

sections.title: PHQ-9 Psychometric Properties
sections.text:
A recent study that employed a non-clinical sample of 58, 272 individuals from multiple countries (Mean age = 43, SD = 13, 63% female) found that the PHQ-9 consisted of a unidimensional structure and the general factor was found to be strong (e.g., factor loadings ranged from 0.725 to 0.893 in the pooled sample) (Bianchi et al., 2022).
To establish reliability and validity, the PHQ-9 was administered to 6,000 patients (pooled mean age = 38.5, SD = 14.32, 83% women) in 8 primary care clinics and 7 obstetrics-gynecology clinics, and construct validity and criterion validity were assessed against independent measures (Kroenke et al., 2001). Criterion validity was assessed against an independent structured mental health professional interview in a sample of 580 patients. The PHQ-9 demonstrates strong convergent validity, correlating with the Brief Beck Depression Inventory ( r = 0.73, p <.0001) and the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12; r = 0.59, p <.0001). Divergent validity is indicated by a lower correlation with quality of life (EuroQOL; r = -0.50, p <.0001), suggesting a stronger link to mental health than general health perceptions (Martin et al., 2006).
The PHQ-9 also demonstrated excellent reliability, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.89, indicating strong internal consistency. Additionally, test-retest reliability over a 48-hour period yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.84, suggesting stability in repeated administrations (Kroenke et al., 2001).
Using a cut-off score of 10, the PHQ-9 performance in detecting depression varies by severity. For major depression, the sensitivity is 81.4%, meaning the PHQ-9 correctly identifies 81.4% of individuals who truly have the condition. The specificity is 89.6%, indicating that it accurately detects 89.6% of those who do not have major depression. The Positive Predictive Value (PPV) is 92.2%, suggesting that when the test indicates a positive result, there is a 92.2% chance the individual actually has major depression. The Negative Predictive Value (NPV) is 76%, implying that a negative result corresponds to a 76% likelihood that the person does not have the condition. For moderate depression, sensitivity increases to 90.6%, with a specificity of 84.5%, PPV of 85.6%, and NPV of 89.9% (Urtasun et al., 2019).
When using the PHQ-9 to track symptoms over time, a significant change in score is defined as an increase or decrease of 5 or more points.
Major Depression (n = 41) Mean = 17.1 SD = 6.1
Other Depressive Disorder (n = 65) Mean = 10.4 SD = 5.4
Percentiles are produced based on a normative community sample consisting of 5,018 individuals from the general population (age range: 14-92 years, 53.6% female), representing a broad demographic distribution (Kocalevent et al., 2013). The study reported that 76.4% of the sample had a score of between 0 to 4, 18% had a score of between 5 and 9, 4.3% had a score of between 10 to 14, and 1.3% had a score of 15+.

sections.text:
The percentile table below illustrates how total scores (see Table 1) compare to individuals in the community, individuals with other depressive disorder, and those with major depression (Kroenke et al., 2001; Kocalevent et al., 2013). Each score is accompanied by a corresponding percentile, indicating the percentage of individuals who scored the same or lower. For instance, a total score of 5 corresponds to the 80th percentile in the normative community sample, 16th percentile in the sample of people with other depressive disorder, and the 2nd percentile in the major depression sample (Table 1). This score signifies that 80% of the individuals in the general population had a score of 5 or lower, whereas only 2% of people with major depression. These graphs provide an understanding of a respondent’s standing relative to the normative community sample, those with other depressive disorder, and compared to individuals with major depression.
