sections.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Child Self Report (ChOCI-R-S)
sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) is a 38-item self-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by the child or adolescent and measures both the obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours they experience and the impairment these cause in daily life. There is also a parent-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-P ) that can be completed by a parent or caregiver.
6 minutes
Ages 7 to 17 years
Adolescent , Child , Diagnosis , OCD

sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

sections.title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
sections.text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-S is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range, and younger children may find a self-report questionnaire hard to complete; the parent-report ChOCI-R-P is a useful alternative. Above age 17, an adult OCD measure such as the OCI-R would typically be more appropriate.

sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-S administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
sections.text: For active CBT-with-ERP, ChOCI-R-S administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether overt rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used to screen for or confirm a diagnosis of OCD?
sections.text: No. The ChOCI-R-S measures OCD symptom content and severity; it is not a diagnostic or screening instrument. It is intended for young people with known or suspected OCD, and its scores are referenced against an OCD-diagnosed sample rather than the general population. Diagnosis should rest on clinical assessment, and where the aim is to detect possible OCD in an unselected group, a dedicated screening measure is more appropriate.

sections.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
sections.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

sections.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
sections.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.

sections.title: Understanding OCD in Young People
sections.text:
According to the DSM-5-TR, OCD is defined by two core features: obsessions and compulsions (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Obsessions are recurrent, unwanted intrusive thoughts or images that cause anxiety or distress; compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to relieve that distress. Common compulsions in children and adolescents include washing, checking, reassurance-seeking, and ordering, counting or repeating until things feel “just right”; common obsessions include thoughts about accidents, death, harm coming to family, doubt, and fears of being bad or upsetting God. These are the symptoms the ChOCI-R-S asks about (Uher et al., 2008). Left untreated, paediatric OCD may disrupt school, friendships and family life and tends to persist into adulthood (Heyman et al., 2006).
Insight typically develops with age. Younger children in particular may have limited or variable awareness of their OCD symptoms, and may not be able to articulate the obsession behind a ritual. Comorbid conditions are also common in paediatric OCD and can complicate assessment, as overlapping symptoms make it harder to attribute presentations to OCD specifically (Stiede et al., 2024). Family members may accommodate OCD symptoms, which can mask how often rituals occur and how much time they take. The parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) captures this observer perspective, complementing the self-report’s fuller access to the young person’s internal experience.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Dimensions
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S comprises six scored outputs across two construct dimensions:
Total Symptoms combines compulsion and obsession symptom scores to reflect the overall complexity and pervasiveness of OCD symptomatology Compulsion Symptoms measures the presence and range of common compulsive behaviours such as hand-washing, checking, ordering, counting, and reassurance-seeking Obsession Symptoms measures the presence and range of common intrusive thoughts, including thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous thoughts, and aggressive or immoral content
Total Impairment combines the two impairment subscales to reflect overall OCD-related functional disruption, and is designed to be comparable to the clinician-rated CY-BOCS total. Compulsion Impairment measures the functional disruption associated with compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friendships, distress, resistance, control, and avoidance Obsession Impairment measures the equivalent functional disruption associated with obsessions
Example ChOCI-R-S Item

sections.title: Clinical Application of the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-S is designed for use with children and adolescents who have an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD. Its main uses fall into three areas:
Assessment and progress monitoring. At baseline, it quantifies symptom breadth and functional impairment to establish OCD severity. Its primary application is progress monitoring during treatment for paediatric OCD, where pre-treatment, mid-treatment and post-treatment scores can be compared to track symptom reduction and functional improvement.
Guiding formulation and treatment focus. The subscale structure can guide where a clinician focuses exposure hierarchies and cognitive intervention. The symptom and impairment profile contributes to a broader case conceptualisation alongside diagnostic interview.
Combining self- and parent-report. Pairing the self-report with the parent-report version (ChOCI-R-P) provides a more comprehensive assessment than either informant alone. A parent adds an observer’s view of how often rituals occur and how much time they take up, which a young person may minimise or not think to mention. Where the two accounts differ, that gap is often the most useful part: it can flag symptoms the young person under-reports, or point to differences in insight and how much the family is accommodating the OCD.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Scoring
sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures both symptoms and impairment:
Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young person to describe their three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not included in the scoring, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Percentiles
sections.text: Each raw score is presented with a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample. A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of young people with OCD in the reference group. Because the norms come from an OCD-diagnosed sample, a low percentile does not mean a young person does not have OCD, only that their symptoms or impairment are milder than most others with the condition.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity / Descriptor Categories
sections.text:
Each of the six scores is reported with a severity descriptor alongside its percentile.
Symptoms: A Low label (green) indicates a symptom level lower than typical for young people with OCD (atypically light for this reference group); Moderate (yellow) indicates a symptom level within the typical range for young people with OCD; High (red) indicates a symptom level above the typical OCD-clinical range. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Symptoms cut-offs:
Total Symptoms : Low 0–9, Moderate 10–25, High 26–40
Compulsion Symptoms : Low 0–5, Moderate 6–13, High 14–20
Obsession Symptoms : Low 0–2, Moderate 3–13, High 14–20
Impairment: A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for young people with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs:
Total Impairment : Minimal 0–9, Mild 10–19, Moderate 20–29, Severe 30–39, Extreme 40–48
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal 0–5, Mild 6–10, Moderate 11–15, Severe 16–20, Extreme 21–24
Obsession Impairment : Minimal 0–2, Mild 3–8, Moderate 9–14, Severe 15–20, Extreme 21–24

sections.title: Subscale interpretation of the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: Each ChOCI-R-S subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the young person reports more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, such as washing, checking, ordering, counting and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous content, or aggressive or immoral content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Graphs
sections.text:
On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).
On repeat administration, the report presents the same results table followed by a 2×3 grid of multi-administration raw-score line plots organised by construct: top row Symptoms (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions); bottom row Impairment (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions). Each plot shows one score over time on its own descriptor bands, so the shading behind each point matches that score’s descriptor in the results table. Unlike the first-administration charts, these graphs emphasise longitudinal change rather than position within the clinical reference distribution.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Development
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R is a revision of the original CHOCI (Shafran et al., 2003), refined to improve item-level psychometrics and broaden severity coverage. The original CHOCI used 19 symptom items rated on a three-point scale (1 to 3) and a 10-item impairment scale derived from the CY-BOCS interview (Goodman et al., 1989; Scahill et al., 1997), scored 0 to 4. The CHOCI-R retains the 10 best-performing symptom items per section (compulsions and obsessions), changes the symptom response format to a three-option scale scored 0 to 2, and adds an avoidance item to each impairment section to align with the adult Y-BOCS. The remaining five impairment items (time, interference, distress, resistance, control) are unchanged between the original CHOCI and the ChOCI-R (Uher et al., 2008).
Published reports describe the ChOCI-R-S as a 32-item measure (the scored items only).
Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

sections.title: Factor Structure of the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: Formal factor analysis was conducted on the 12 impairment items, which underpin the measure’s severity scoring; the symptom items were evaluated using internal consistency rather than factor analysis (Uher et al., 2008). For the self-report version, a single common factor explained 46% of the variance in the impairment items, largely because the two resistance items loaded poorly; removing them increased the explained variance to 53%. Exploratory factor analysis further supported separate Obsession and Compulsion dimensions, with the resistance items forming a distinct factor.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Reliability
sections.text: Internal consistency of the ChOCI-R-S was good across the four subscales and two totals (Uher et al., 2008). For the impairment scales, Cronbach’s alpha was .82 (Obsessions Impairment, N = 249), .76 (Compulsions Impairment, N = 278) and .86 (Total Impairment, N = 244). For the symptom scales, alpha was .86 (Obsession Symptoms, N = 258), .72 (Compulsion Symptoms, N = 261) and .84 (Total Symptoms, N = 257). The lower alpha for the Compulsion Symptoms scale reflects the heterogeneity of compulsive behaviours (washing, checking, ordering, counting), which need not co-occur within a child. On the impairment scales, the two resistance items had low item-total correlations; with them removed, alpha rose to .86 (obsessions), .80 (compulsions) and .88 (total).

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Validity
sections.text:
Convergent validity was demonstrated through moderate correlation between the ChOCI-R-S Total Impairment and the CY-BOCS Total score ( r = 0.55, N = 211, p < .001; Uher et al., 2008). This was numerically higher than the correlation for the parent-report version ( r = 0.45), although the difference between the two was not statistically significant.
Evidence for divergent validity is more mixed. Across the self- and parent-report versions, ChOCI-R severity scores correlated moderately with the SDQ emotional-problems subscale ( r = 0.30–0.51), weakly with conduct problems ( r = 0.11–0.22) and intermediately with hyperactivity ( r = 0.26–0.32) (Uher et al., 2008). Rapp and colleagues (2016) rated divergent validity as good from externalising problems but only fair to poor from emotional disorders. For the original ChOCI, sensitivity (88%) and specificity (95%) against non-clinical controls were high, but these have not been examined for the revised measure (Rapp et al., 2016).
Agreement between ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P was strong, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69–0.83) for Total Impairment, 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.77) for Obsessions Impairment, and 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.85) for Compulsions Impairment (Uher et al., 2008).

sections.title: Sensitivity to Change for the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: The best available data on the ChOCI-R-S’s sensitivity to change come from Lenhard and colleagues (2017), a randomised trial of internet-delivered CBT in adolescents aged 12 to 17 ( N = 67) in which the ChOCI-R-S was a secondary outcome. It reported a within-group pre-post effect of d = 0.57 (95% CI 0.16–0.98) and a between-group effect of d = 0.64 (95% CI 0.11–1.16) favouring internet-delivered CBT over waitlist ( p = .014), with continued improvement to a 3-month follow-up. This is encouraging but preliminary: a single trial, in adolescents only.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations is interpreted via a Reliable Change Index (RCI) computed with the Jacobson-Truax formula, using the Uher and colleagues (2008) self-report internal consistency reliability and standard deviation for each total. A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment (alpha = .86, SD = 8.7), or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms (alpha = .84, SD = 7.8), exceeds measurement error at the 95% confidence level and is interpreted as a reliable change.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Sample Data
sections.text: Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity Descriptors
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-S scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997).

Obsession Symptoms : Low 0–2, Moderate 3–13, High 14–20
Impairment: A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for young people with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs:
Total Impairment : Minimal 0–9, Mild 10–19, Moderate 20–29, Severe 30–39, Extreme 40–48
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal 0–5, Mild 6–10, Moderate 11–15, Severe 16–20, Extreme 21–24
Obsession Impairment : Minimal 0–2, Mild 3–8, Moderate 9–14, Severe 15–20, Extreme 21–24

sections.title: Subscale interpretation of the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: Each ChOCI-R-S subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the young person reports more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, such as washing, checking, ordering, counting and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, doubt, death, religious or blasphemous content, or aggressive or immoral content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Graphs
sections.text:
On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score on a 0–40 axis for Symptoms or 0–48 for Impairment. A clinical 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average show the score relative to the clinical reference sample of young people with OCD. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession bars on a 0–20 axis for Symptoms or 0–24 for Impairment, each with its own 25th-to-75th reference rectangle and clinical-average line). Beneath each bar, a coloured strip marks that scale’s descriptor bands (Low, Moderate and High for Symptoms; Minimal, Mild, Moderate, Severe and Extreme for Impairment, with Minimal shown in white).
On repeat administration, the report presents the same results table followed by a 2×3 grid of multi-administration raw-score line plots organised by construct: top row Symptoms (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions); bottom row Impairment (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions). Each plot shows one score over time on its own descriptor bands, so the shading behind each point matches that score’s descriptor in the results table. Unlike the first-administration charts, these graphs emphasise longitudinal change rather than position within the clinical reference distribution.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Development
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R is a revision of the original CHOCI (Shafran et al., 2003), refined to improve item-level psychometrics and broaden severity coverage. The original CHOCI used 19 symptom items rated on a three-point scale (1 to 3) and a 10-item impairment scale derived from the CY-BOCS interview (Goodman et al., 1989; Scahill et al., 1997), scored 0 to 4. The CHOCI-R retains the 10 best-performing symptom items per section (compulsions and obsessions), changes the symptom response format to a three-option scale scored 0 to 2, and adds an avoidance item to each impairment section to align with the adult Y-BOCS. The remaining five impairment items (time, interference, distress, resistance, control) are unchanged between the original CHOCI and the ChOCI-R (Uher et al., 2008).
Published reports describe the ChOCI-R-S as a 32-item measure (the scored items only).
Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

sections.title: Factor Structure of the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: Formal factor analysis was conducted on the 12 impairment items, which underpin the measure’s severity scoring; the symptom items were evaluated using internal consistency rather than factor analysis (Uher et al., 2008). For the self-report version, a single common factor explained 46% of the variance in the impairment items, largely because the two resistance items loaded poorly; removing them increased the explained variance to 53%. Exploratory factor analysis further supported separate Obsession and Compulsion dimensions, with the resistance items forming a distinct factor.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Reliability
sections.text: Internal consistency of the ChOCI-R-S was good across the four subscales and two totals (Uher et al., 2008). For the impairment scales, Cronbach’s alpha was .82 (Obsessions Impairment, N = 249), .76 (Compulsions Impairment, N = 278) and .86 (Total Impairment, N = 244). For the symptom scales, alpha was .86 (Obsession Symptoms, N = 258), .72 (Compulsion Symptoms, N = 261) and .84 (Total Symptoms, N = 257). The lower alpha for the Compulsion Symptoms scale reflects the heterogeneity of compulsive behaviours (washing, checking, ordering, counting), which need not co-occur within a child. On the impairment scales, the two resistance items had low item-total correlations; with them removed, alpha rose to .86 (obsessions), .80 (compulsions) and .88 (total).

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Validity
sections.text:
Convergent validity was demonstrated through moderate correlation between the ChOCI-R-S Total Impairment and the CY-BOCS Total score ( r = 0.55, N = 211, p < .001; Uher et al., 2008). This was numerically higher than the correlation for the parent-report version ( r = 0.45), although the difference between the two was not statistically significant.
Evidence for divergent validity is more mixed. Across the self- and parent-report versions, ChOCI-R severity scores correlated moderately with the SDQ emotional-problems subscale ( r = 0.30–0.51), weakly with conduct problems ( r = 0.11–0.22) and intermediately with hyperactivity ( r = 0.26–0.32) (Uher et al., 2008). Rapp and colleagues (2016) rated divergent validity as good from externalising problems but only fair to poor from emotional disorders. For the original ChOCI, sensitivity (88%) and specificity (95%) against non-clinical controls were high, but these have not been examined for the revised measure (Rapp et al., 2016).
Agreement between ChOCI-R-S and ChOCI-R-P was strong, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69–0.83) for Total Impairment, 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.77) for Obsessions Impairment, and 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.85) for Compulsions Impairment (Uher et al., 2008).

sections.title: Sensitivity to Change for the ChOCI-R-S
sections.text: The best available data on the ChOCI-R-S’s sensitivity to change come from Lenhard and colleagues (2017), a randomised trial of internet-delivered CBT in adolescents aged 12 to 17 ( N = 67) in which the ChOCI-R-S was a secondary outcome. It reported a within-group pre-post effect of d = 0.57 (95% CI 0.16–0.98) and a between-group effect of d = 0.64 (95% CI 0.11–1.16) favouring internet-delivered CBT over waitlist ( p = .014), with continued improvement to a 3-month follow-up. This is encouraging but preliminary: a single trial, in adolescents only.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Change Score Interpretation
sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-S is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations is interpreted via a Reliable Change Index (RCI) computed with the Jacobson-Truax formula, using the Uher and colleagues (2008) self-report internal consistency reliability and standard deviation for each total. A change of approximately 9.0 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment (alpha = .86, SD = 8.7), or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms (alpha = .84, SD = 7.8), exceeds measurement error at the 95% confidence level and is interpreted as a reliable change.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Sample Data
sections.text: Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (244 to 278 with complete self-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ age M = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ age M = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the self-report subscales are: Compulsion Symptoms M = 9.5, SD = 4.3; Obsession Symptoms M = 8.0, SD = 5.1; Total Symptoms M = 17.6, SD = 7.8; Compulsion Impairment M = 15.0, SD = 4.5; Obsession Impairment M = 13.5, SD = 5.2; Total Impairment M = 28.5, SD = 8.7. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a young person diagnosed with OCD, not the general population. No community-sample reference data exists for the self-report ChOCI-R-S, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

sections.title: ChOCI-R-S Severity Descriptors
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-S scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997).

sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

sections.title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
sections.text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-S is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range, and younger children may find a self-report questionnaire hard to complete; the parent-report ChOCI-R-P is a useful alternative. Above age 17, an adult OCD measure such as the OCI-R would typically be more appropriate.

sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-S administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
sections.text: For active CBT-with-ERP, ChOCI-R-S administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether overt rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used to screen for or confirm a diagnosis of OCD?
sections.text: No. The ChOCI-R-S measures OCD symptom content and severity; it is not a diagnostic or screening instrument. It is intended for young people with known or suspected OCD, and its scores are referenced against an OCD-diagnosed sample rather than the general population. Diagnosis should rest on clinical assessment, and where the aim is to detect possible OCD in an unselected group, a dedicated screening measure is more appropriate.

sections.title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
sections.text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

sections.title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
sections.text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.

sourceGuidance.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory – Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) Scoring
sourceGuidance.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Self Report (ChOCI-R-S) produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The ChOCI-R-S measures both symptoms and impairment:
Total Symptoms (sum of Compulsion Symptoms and Obsession Symptoms; scores range from 0 to 40) Compulsion Symptoms (items 1 to 10; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items Obsession Symptoms (items 20 to 29; scores range from 0 to 20): sum of 10 items
Total Impairment (sum of Compulsion Impairment and Obsession Impairment; scores range from 0 to 48) Compulsion Impairment (items 14 to 19; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items Obsession Impairment (items 33 to 38; scores range from 0 to 24): sum of 6 items
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the young person to describe their three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not included in the scoring, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

records.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory- Revised-Parent (ChOCI-R-P)
records.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) is a 38-item parent-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by a parent or caregiver who is familiar with the child’s experiences. There is also a self-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-S ) that can be completed by children or adolescents aged 7 to 17 years.
records.administration: Each of the following questions asks you about things or “habits” you feel your child has to do although they may know that they do not make sense. Sometimes, they may try to stop from doing them but this might not be possible. They might feel worried or angry or frustrated until they have finished what they have to do. An example of a habit like this may be the need to wash their hands over and over again even though they are not really dirty, or the need to count up to a special number (e.g. 6 or 10) while they do certain things. Please answer each question by choosing how much you agree with the statement, or how much you think it is true of your child. Please answer each item, without spending too much time on any one item. sections.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory- Revised-Parent (ChOCI-R-P)
sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) is a 38-item parent-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by a parent or caregiver who is familiar with the child’s experiences. There is also a self-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-S ) that can be completed by children or adolescents aged 7 to 17 years.
6 minutes
Ages 7 to 17 years
Adolescent , Child , Diagnosis , OCD

sections.title: How should I interpret a profile where Symptoms and Impairment scores diverge?
sections.text: Symptoms and Impairment measure related but distinct dimensions: how often and how strongly symptoms are present, and how much they disrupt daily life. The two can move independently and the gap itself is informative. Where symptoms are elevated but impairment is lower, possible explanations include early presentation, effective coping strategies, or family routines that accommodate symptoms in ways that buffer functional impact. The reverse profile (lower symptoms with elevated impairment) may indicate that the symptoms present are particularly entrenched or distressing, or that the parent is observing functional effects without fully identifying the underlying symptoms. Both divergent profiles warrant looking beyond the totals during formulation.

sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child-rated ChOCI-R-S?
sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-P be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-P is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. One small treatment study has used it with children as young as 5 (Chessell et al., 2024). Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range. The reference sample included 18-year-olds, so the measure can be used at this age, though a self-report adult measure such as the OCI-R may be more appropriate.

sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-P administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
sections.text: For active CBT-with-Exposure and Response Prevention, parent-rated ChOCI-R-P administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether observable rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence. Trial protocols have used both weekly and pre/post/3-month schedules.

sections.title: Should I use the ChOCI-R-P alongside the child-report version?
sections.text: Yes, where the child is able to complete a self-report. The parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child self-rated ChOCI-R-S are most powerful when used together: administering both at initial assessment gives the clinician a multi-informant baseline that supports more confident formulation and treatment planning. During active treatment, the two measures can be used flexibly. Weekly or fortnightly ChOCI-R-P is the typical pattern for tracking observable change, with periodic ChOCI-R-S to check whether the child’s own experience is shifting alongside the behavioural picture. For younger children who cannot reliably self-report, the ChOCI-R-P alone remains a strong progress-monitoring tool.

sections.title: How are the severity descriptors set, and what do they mean?
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
(2008), with each band starting at the next whole score.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) General Overview
sections.text:
OCD in children and adolescents is characterised by recurrent unwanted thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) that the child feels compelled to perform. If untreated, paediatric OCD is associated with substantial functional impairment in academic, social and family domains and tends to persist into adulthood (Heyman et al., 2006). Reliable measurement of severity in young people is challenging because children may under-report or over-report their symptoms during clinical interview, and parents often have observable information about compulsions (washing, checking, ordering) that the child cannot articulate. A parent-report measure offers a useful complement to a child-report, particularly for younger children and for tracking change over time.
The ChOCI-R-P comprises six scored outputs across two construct dimensions:
1. Compulsion Symptoms: frequency and presence of compulsive behaviours (hand-washing, checking, ordering, counting, reassurance-seeking)
2. Obsession Symptoms: frequency and presence of intrusive thoughts (harm, contamination, doubt, blasphemy, aggression)
3. Total Symptoms: overall complexity and pervasiveness of OCD symptomatology
4. Compulsion Impairment: functional disruption from compulsions (time spent, interference, distress, resistance, control, avoidance)
5. Obsession Impairment: equivalent functional disruption from obsessions
6. Total Impairment: overall OCD-related functional disruption
Example ChOCI-R-P Item

sections.title: Clinical Application of the ChOCI-R-P
sections.text: The measure is designed for use with children and adolescents who have an established or suspected diagnosis of OCD. Its primary application is progress monitoring during treatment for paediatric OCD, where pre-treatment, mid-treatment and post-treatment scores can be compared to track symptom reduction and functional improvement. The subscale structure of the ChOCI-R-P can also guide where a clinician focuses exposure hierarchies and cognitive intervention. Additionally, the measure can inform formulation, where the symptom and impairment profile contributes to a broader case conceptualisation alongside diagnostic interview and child-report data.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) Scoring
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R-P produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The measure produces two parallel sets of scores: symptoms (how often and how strongly OCD presents) and impairment (how much OCD disrupts daily life).
Total Symptoms : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Symptoms (range 0–40) Compulsion Symptoms : sum of items 1 to 10 (range 0–20) Obsession Symptoms : sum of items 20 to 29 (range 0–20)
Total Impairment : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Impairment (range 0–48) Compulsion Impairment : sum of items 14 to 19 (range 0–24) Obsession Impairment : sum of items 33 to 38 (range 0–24)
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the parent to describe the child’s three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not scored, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Percentiles
sections.text: Each raw score is presented alongside a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample (Uher et al., 2008). A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of OCD-diagnosed children in the reference group. Because the reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a child diagnosed with OCD, not the general paediatric population.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Severity Descriptors
sections.text:
Each of the six scores is reported with a severity descriptor alongside its percentile. The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement.
Symptoms (three bands): A Low label (green) indicates a symptom level lower than typical for children with OCD (atypically light for this reference group); Moderate (yellow) indicates a symptom level within the typical range for children with OCD; High (red) indicates a symptom level above the typical OCD-clinical range. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Symptoms cut-offs. Raw-score boundaries:
Total Symptoms : Low ≤10, Moderate 11–26, High ≥27
Compulsion Symptoms : Low ≤5, Moderate 6–14, High ≥15
Obsession Symptoms : Low ≤3, Moderate 4–13, High ≥14
Impairment (five bands): A Minimal label (white) indicates functional disruption lower than typical for children with OCD; Mild (green) indicates mild functional disruption relative to the OCD-clinical reference; Moderate (yellow) indicates functional disruption within the typical OCD-clinical range; Severe (orange) indicates functional disruption in the middle-to-upper portion of the OCD-clinical reference distribution; Extreme (red) indicates functional disruption among the highest levels observed in the OCD-clinical reference distribution. Each subscale has its own cut-offs, placed at the same position in the reference sample as the Total Impairment cut-offs. Raw-score boundaries:
Total Impairment : Minimal ≤13, Mild 14–23, Moderate 24–33, Severe 34–42, Extreme ≥43
Compulsion Impairment : Minimal ≤7, Mild 8–12, Moderate 13–17, Severe 18–21, Extreme ≥22
Obsession Impairment : Minimal ≤4, Mild 5–10, Moderate 11–16, Severe 17–21, Extreme ≥22

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Subscale Interpretation
sections.text: Each subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the parent has observed more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, including washing, checking, ordering, counting, repeating, and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, contamination, doubt, mortality, blasphemy, or aggressive content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Change Score Interpretation
sections.text: When the ChOCI-R-P is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 8.4 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Graphs
sections.text:
On first administration, the report presents a results table followed by two construct sections (Symptoms and Impairment). Each section contains two horizontal raw-score charts. The first plots the construct’s total as a single bar with the client’s raw score against a 25th-to-75th percentile reference rectangle and a dashed line at the clinical average from the OCD-clinical reference sample. The second plots the construct’s two subscales (Compulsion and Obsession) with their own reference rectangles and clinical-average lines.
On repeat administration, the report presents the same results table followed by a 2×3 grid of multi-administration raw-score line plots organised by construct: top row Symptoms (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions); bottom row Impairment (Total, Compulsions, Obsessions). Each plot shows one score over time on its own descriptor bands, so the shading behind each point matches that score’s descriptor in the results table. Unlike the first-administration charts, these graphs emphasise longitudinal change rather than position within the clinical reference distribution.

sections.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) Development
sections.text:
The ChOCI-R is a revision of the original CHOCI (Shafran et al., 2003), refined to improve item-level psychometrics and broaden severity coverage. The original CHOCI used 19 symptom items rated on a three-point scale (1 to 3) and a 10-item impairment scale derived from the CY-BOCS interview (Goodman et al., 1989; Scahill et al., 1997), scored 0 to 4. The ChOCI-R retains the 10 best-performing symptom items per section (compulsions and obsessions), changes the symptom response format to a three-option scale scored 0 to 2, and adds an avoidance item to each impairment section to align with the adult Y-BOCS. The remaining five impairment items (time, interference, distress, resistance, control) are unchanged between the original CHOCI and the ChOCI-R (Uher et al., 2008).
Published reports describe the ChOCI-R-P as a 32-item measure (the scored items only).
Psychometric validation of the ChOCI-R was conducted in a sample of 285 children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic over the period 2000 to 2006 (Uher et al., 2008). All children met ICD-10 criteria for OCD established via structured clinical interview.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Factor Structure
sections.text: Factor-analytic work supports the use of separate Compulsion and Obsession subscales for clinical interpretation. Exploratory analysis of the ChOCI-R-P recovered three factors broadly corresponding to Compulsions, Obsessions and Resistance, with the parent version showing less clean obsession/compulsion separation than the self-report version (Uher et al., 2008). This pattern is consistent with parents inferring obsessions from observed behaviours rather than directly accessing the child’s internal experience.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Reliability
sections.text: Internal consistency of the ChOCI-R-P is strong across the four subscales and two totals (Uher et al., 2008). For the impairment scales, Cronbach’s α was .84 (Obsessions Impairment, N = 240), .78 (Compulsions Impairment, N = 269) and .87 (Total Impairment, N = 240). For the symptom scales, α was .86 (Obsession Symptoms, N = 240), .75 (Compulsion Symptoms, N = 269) and .85 (Total Symptoms, N = 240). The lower α for the Compulsion Symptoms scale reflects the heterogeneity of compulsive behaviours, with the hand-washing item showing a low item-total correlation; the authors retained the item to preserve coverage of a clinically common compulsion.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Validity
sections.text:
Convergent validity was demonstrated through a moderate correlation between the ChOCI-R-P Total Impairment and the CY-BOCS Total score ( r = 0.45, N = 199, p < .001; Uher et al., 2008). The moderate (rather than strong) correlation, compared with r = 0.55 for the ChOCI-R-S against the CY-BOCS, reflects the partial independence of parent observation and clinician-rated severity in young people.
Inter-rater agreement between ChOCI-R-P and ChOCI-R-S was strong, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.77 (95% CI 0.69–0.83) for Total Impairment, 0.70 (95% CI 0.59–0.77) for Obsessions Impairment, and 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.85) for Compulsions Impairment (Uher et al., 2008).
Item-response theory (IRT) analysis demonstrated that the parent-report ChOCI-R-P provides better discrimination across the mild-to-moderate severity range than the CY-BOCS interview, which discriminates best at the most severe end of the spectrum (Uher et al., 2008). This complementary discriminatory profile supports the use of the ChOCI-R-P as a routine outcome measure in clinical practice, where many children present in the mild-to-moderate severity range and finer-grained discrimination is clinically useful.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Sensitivity to Change
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-P has demonstrated sensitivity to change in three independent treatment studies spanning the paediatric age range (7 to 17). Lenhard and colleagues (2017) reported a within-group pre-post effect of d = 0.68 (95% CI 0.18–1.18) and a between-group effect of d = 0.59 (95% CI 0.09–1.10) favouring internet-delivered CBT over waitlist in adolescents aged 12 to 17 ( N = 67; p = .012), with continued improvement to a 3-month follow-up. Aspvall and colleagues (2018) reported very large pre-post effects ( d = 2.15, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.20) in a 12-week internet-delivered CBT open trial with young children aged 7 to 11 ( N = 11), with α = .87 in that sample (replicating Uher et al., 2008). Chessell and colleagues (2024) reported large pre-post effects in a parent-led brief CBT case series of pre-adolescents aged 5 to 12 ( N = 10): d ≈ −1.0 for symptoms and d ≈ −1.1 for impairment, with 50% reliable improvement on symptoms and 60% on impairment at post-treatment.

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Descriptors
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 17th percentile and High at about the 85th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 58th and Extreme about the 89th.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997).

sections.title: ChOCI-R-P Sample Data
sections.text: Reference percentiles are derived from Uher and colleagues (2008): 285 consecutive referrals (240 to 269 with complete parent-report data per subscale) to an OCD clinic between 2000 and 2006, all meeting ICD-10 criteria for OCD via structured clinical interview, with no significant sex differences (boys’ average age = 13.7, range 7 to 18; girls’ average age = 13.7, range 9 to 18). Reference parameters for the parent-report subscales are Compulsion Symptoms average = 9.8, SD = 4.5; Obsession Symptoms average = 8.4, SD = 5.2; Total Symptoms average = 18.3, SD = 8.0; Compulsion Impairment average = 16.5, SD = 4.2; Obsession Impairment average = 15.5, SD = 5.0; Total Impairment average = 32.1, SD = 8.4. Because this reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed reference group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a child diagnosed with OCD, not the general paediatric population. No community-sample reference data exists for the parent-report ChOCI-R-P, and the original authors note that confirmation in primary care and population-based samples remains needed (Uher et al., 2008).

sections.title: How should I interpret a profile where Symptoms and Impairment scores diverge?
sections.text: Symptoms and Impairment measure related but distinct dimensions: how often and how strongly symptoms are present, and how much they disrupt daily life. The two can move independently and the gap itself is informative. Where symptoms are elevated but impairment is lower, possible explanations include early presentation, effective coping strategies, or family routines that accommodate symptoms in ways that buffer functional impact. The reverse profile (lower symptoms with elevated impairment) may indicate that the symptoms present are particularly entrenched or distressing, or that the parent is observing functional effects without fully identifying the underlying symptoms. Both divergent profiles warrant looking beyond the totals during formulation.

sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child-rated ChOCI-R-S?
sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-P be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-P is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. One small treatment study has used it with children as young as 5 (Chessell et al., 2024). Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range. The reference sample included 18-year-olds, so the measure can be used at this age, though a self-report adult measure such as the OCI-R may be more appropriate.

sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-P administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
sections.text: For active CBT-with-Exposure and Response Prevention, parent-rated ChOCI-R-P administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether observable rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence. Trial protocols have used both weekly and pre/post/3-month schedules.

sections.title: Should I use the ChOCI-R-P alongside the child-report version?
sections.text: Yes, where the child is able to complete a self-report. The parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child self-rated ChOCI-R-S are most powerful when used together: administering both at initial assessment gives the clinician a multi-informant baseline that supports more confident formulation and treatment planning. During active treatment, the two measures can be used flexibly. Weekly or fortnightly ChOCI-R-P is the typical pattern for tracking observable change, with periodic ChOCI-R-S to check whether the child’s own experience is shifting alongside the behavioural picture. For younger children who cannot reliably self-report, the ChOCI-R-P alone remains a strong progress-monitoring tool.

sections.title: How are the severity descriptors set, and what do they mean?
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). sourceGuidance.title: Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) Scoring
sourceGuidance.text:
The ChOCI-R-P produces six raw scores by summing item responses. Higher scores indicate more obsessive-compulsive symptoms or greater associated functional impairment. The measure produces two parallel sets of scores: symptoms (how often and how strongly OCD presents) and impairment (how much OCD disrupts daily life).
Total Symptoms : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Symptoms (range 0–40) Compulsion Symptoms : sum of items 1 to 10 (range 0–20) Obsession Symptoms : sum of items 20 to 29 (range 0–20)
Total Impairment : sum of Compulsion and Obsession Impairment (range 0–48) Compulsion Impairment : sum of items 14 to 19 (range 0–24) Obsession Impairment : sum of items 33 to 38 (range 0–24)
Six open-text items (items 11 to 13 for habits and items 30 to 32 for thoughts) ask the parent to describe the child’s three most upsetting habits (compulsions) and thoughts (obsessions), respectively. These items are not scored, but provide additional clinical information to inform assessment and treatment planning.

sourceGuidance.title: ChOCI-R-P Percentiles
sourceGuidance.text: Each raw score is presented alongside a percentile rank against an OCD-clinical reference sample (Uher et al., 2008). A percentile of 50 corresponds to the OCD-clinical reference average; a percentile of 80 indicates a score exceeding approximately 80% of OCD-diagnosed children in the reference group. Because the reference sample is clinical (not community), percentile interpretation is positional within an OCD-diagnosed group: a percentile of 50 reflects the average level for a child diagnosed with OCD, not the general paediatric population.

sourceGuidance.title: ChOCI-R-P Subscale Interpretation
sourceGuidance.text: Each subscale assesses a different aspect of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or associated impairment. Higher scores on Compulsion Symptoms indicate that the parent has observed more frequent or more severe compulsive behaviours, including washing, checking, ordering, counting, repeating, and reassurance-seeking. Higher scores on Obsession Symptoms indicate more frequent intrusive thoughts of harm, contamination, doubt, mortality, blasphemy, or aggressive content. Higher scores on Compulsion Impairment indicate greater functional disruption from compulsions, including time spent, interference with school and friends, distress when prevented from acting, difficulty resisting or controlling compulsions, and avoidance. Higher scores on Obsession Impairment indicate similar impacts associated with obsessive thoughts.

sourceGuidance.title: ChOCI-R-P Change Score Interpretation
sourceGuidance.text: When the ChOCI-R-P is administered on multiple occasions, change between administrations can be evaluated using a Reliable Change Index (RCI). A change of approximately 8.4 raw-score points or greater on Total Impairment, or 8.6 or greater on Total Symptoms, indicates a change that is unlikely to be attributable to measurement error alone.

Where symptoms are elevated but impairment is lower, possible explanations include early presentation, effective coping strategies, or family routines that accommodate symptoms in ways that buffer functional impact. The reverse profile (lower symptoms with elevated impairment) may indicate that the symptoms present are particularly entrenched or distressing, or that the parent is observing functional effects without fully identifying the underlying symptoms. Both divergent profiles warrant looking beyond the totals during formulation.

records.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory- Revised-Parent (ChOCI-R-P)
records.description: The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) is a 38-item parent-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by a parent or caregiver who is familiar with the child’s experiences. There is also a self-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-S ) that can be completed by children or adolescents aged 7 to 17 years.
records.administration: Each of the following questions asks you about things or “habits” you feel your child has to do although they may know that they do not make sense. Sometimes, they may try to stop from doing them but this might not be possible. They might feel worried or angry or frustrated until they have finished what they have to do. An example of a habit like this may be the need to wash their hands over and over again even though they are not really dirty, or the need to count up to a special number (e.g. 6 or 10) while they do certain things. Please answer each question by choosing how much you agree with the statement, or how much you think it is true of your child. Please answer each item, without spending too much time on any one item. There are no right or wrong answers. Compulsions· symptoms

sections.title: Obsessional Compulsive Inventory- Revised-Parent (ChOCI-R-P)
sections.text:
The Children’s Obsessional Compulsive Inventory–Revised – Parent Report (ChOCI-R-P) is a 38-item parent-report measure of obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms (Uher et al., 2008) in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. It is completed by a parent or caregiver who is familiar with the child’s experiences. There is also a self-report version of the ChOCI ( ChOCI-R-S ) that can be completed by children or adolescents aged 7 to 17 years.
6 minutes
Ages 7 to 17 years
Adolescent , Child , Diagnosis , OCD

sections.title: How should I interpret a profile where Symptoms and Impairment scores diverge?
sections.text: Symptoms and Impairment measure related but distinct dimensions: how often and how strongly symptoms are present, and how much they disrupt daily life. The two can move independently and the gap itself is informative. Where symptoms are elevated but impairment is lower, possible explanations include early presentation, effective coping strategies, or family routines that accommodate symptoms in ways that buffer functional impact. The reverse profile (lower symptoms with elevated impairment) may indicate that the symptoms present are particularly entrenched or distressing, or that the parent is observing functional effects without fully identifying the underlying symptoms. Both divergent profiles warrant looking beyond the totals during formulation.

sections.title: How should I interpret a large gap between the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child-rated ChOCI-R-S?
sections.text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

sections.title: Can the ChOCI-R-P be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
sections.text: The ChOCI-R-P is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. One small treatment study has used it with children as young as 5 (Chessell et al., 2024). Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range. The reference sample included 18-year-olds, so the measure can be used at this age, though a self-report adult measure such as the OCI-R may be more appropriate.

sections.title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-P administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
sections.text: For active CBT-with-Exposure and Response Prevention, parent-rated ChOCI-R-P administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether observable rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence. Trial protocols have used both weekly and pre/post/3-month schedules.

sections.title: Should I use the ChOCI-R-P alongside the child-report version?
sections.text: Yes, where the child is able to complete a self-report. The parent-rated ChOCI-R-P and the child self-rated ChOCI-R-S are most powerful when used together: administering both at initial assessment gives the clinician a multi-informant baseline that supports more confident formulation and treatment planning. During active treatment, the two measures can be used flexibly. Weekly or fortnightly ChOCI-R-P is the typical pattern for tracking observable change, with periodic ChOCI-R-S to check whether the child’s own experience is shifting alongside the behavioural picture. For younger children who cannot reliably self-report, the ChOCI-R-P alone remains a strong progress-monitoring tool.

sections.title: How are the severity descriptors set, and what do they mean?
sections.text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-P scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study.
(2008), with each band starting at the next whole score.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement.
